title: What is IAM, and what is the difference between an IAM User, an IAM Group, an IAM Role, and an IAM Policy?
shortTitle: IAM — User, Group, Role and Policy

s1_definition.profdef: IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the AWS service that controls who is authenticated and what they are authorized to do. An IAM User is a permanent identity with long-lived credentials (a password and/or access keys) for a human or legacy application. An IAM Group is a collection of Users that share the same permissions, used only to attach policies in one place. An IAM Role is an identity with no long-lived credentials that is assumed temporarily to obtain short-lived credentials from STS. An IAM Policy is a JSON document that lists allowed or denied actions on specific resources and is attached to Users, Groups, or Roles to grant those permissions.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, an IAM User is a permanent staff member like Rajesh with his own ID card and password. An IAM Group is a department like "Tellers" — everyone in it automatically gets the teller permissions. An IAM Role is a temporary visitor badge: a contractor or a machine borrows it for a few hours, does the job, and the badge expires. An IAM Policy is the printed rulebook that says exactly which rooms a badge can open — "may open the cash vault, may not open the manager's office."
s1_definition.oneliner: User is a permanent person, Group bundles people for shared rules, Role is a temporary borrowed identity, and Policy is the rulebook that grants the actual permissions.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the AWS service that controls who is authenticated and what they are authorized to do. An IAM User is a permanent identity with long-lived credentials (a password and/or access keys) for a human or legacy application. An IAM Group is a collection of Users that share the same permissions, used only to attach policies in one place. An IAM Role is an identity with no long-lived credentials that is assumed temporarily to obtain short-lived credentials from STS. An IAM Policy is a JSON document that lists allowed or denied actions on specific resources and is attached to Users, Groups, or Roles to grant those permissions.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, an IAM User is a permanent staff member like Rajesh with his own ID card and password. An IAM Group is a department like "Tellers" — everyone in it automatically gets the teller permissions. An IAM Role is a temporary visitor badge: a contractor or a machine borrows it for a few hours, does the job, and the badge expires. An IAM Policy is the printed rulebook that says exactly which rooms a badge can open — "may open the cash vault, may not open the manager's office."

**One line to remember:** User is a permanent person, Group bundles people for shared rules, Role is a temporary borrowed identity, and Policy is the rulebook that grants the actual permissions.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has twenty engineers who all need the same read access to the statements bucket. Attaching the same policy to twenty Users by hand is error-prone and when the policy changes you must edit twenty places. This is exactly what an IAM Group solves: attach the policy once to the group, add all engineers, and one edit updates everyone.

Problem 2 — The statement-generator service runs on EC2 and must read the bucket. If we bake an access key into the code, a leak is a disaster. This is exactly what an IAM Role solves: the EC2 instance assumes a Role and gets temporary credentials that rotate automatically, so there is no secret to leak.

We will model this with a tiny permission engine: `IamUser`, `IamGroup`, `IamRole`, and `IamPolicy`, plus an `AccessEvaluator` that decides if an action is allowed. Demo: Rajesh the User inherits group permissions, and the service assumes a Role to read the bucket.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one read policy, a Developers group, the User Rajesh, and a service Role.

Step 1 — The `ReadStatements` policy is created once with effect ALLOW on `s3:GetObject` for the statements bucket. It is the single rulebook everyone shares.

Step 2 — The policy is attached to the `Developers` group. The group now carries the read permission, but no one has logged in yet.

Step 3 — Rajesh joins the `Developers` group. When we compute `effectivePolicies()`, we take the union of his inline policies (none) and the group's policies (the read policy). So Rajesh inherits read access without any policy attached directly to him.

Step 4 — The service Role gets the same policy attached directly. When the EC2 instance assumes the Role, it holds that policy through temporary credentials, with no access key in the code.

Step 5 — The `AccessEvaluator` checks both. For each it scans the policies; an explicit deny would win immediately, otherwise an allow match returns true, and no match falls through to the implicit deny. Both Rajesh and the service are allowed.

```
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] User rajesh (via group) can read statement: true
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Service via assumed Role can read statement: true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  IamPolicy "ReadStatements" (ALLOW s3:GetObject on bucket/*)
    │
    ├────────────────→ IamGroup "Developers"
    │                      │ attach
    │                      ▼
    │                   IamUser "rajesh" joinGroup
    │                      │ effectivePolicies() = union(inline, group)
    │                      ▼
    │                   AccessEvaluator.isAllowed(...) → true
    │
    └────────────────→ IamRole "StatementReaderRole"
                           │ EC2 assumeRole via STS → temp creds
                           ▼
                        AccessEvaluator.isAllowed(...) → true
```

```
  ┌─ Patterns ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Composite: User aggregates Group policies + inline      │
  │ Strategy: AccessEvaluator applies deny>allow>implicit    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: IamPolicy only matches; Evaluator only decides        │

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────┐   *  ┌──────────┐  * ┌───────────┐
  │ IamUser  │◇────→│ IamGroup │◇──→│ IamPolicy │
  └──────────┘      └──────────┘    └───────────┘
       │ effectivePolicies()             ▲
       ▼                                 │
  ┌────────────────┐                ┌──────────┐
  │ AccessEvaluator│───────────────→│ IamRole  │◇─┘
  │ + isAllowed()  │                └──────────┘
  └────────────────┘

  Contract for isAllowed(policies, action, resource):
    Pre:  policy list non-null
    Post: explicit DENY → false, matching ALLOW → true, else false
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
IAM is the AWS service that answers two questions for every request: who are you, and what are you allowed to do. The four building blocks are User, Group, Role, and Policy, and the key is understanding which ones are identities and which one is the permission itself. A Policy is the permission — a JSON document that says allow or deny a set of actions on specific resources. It carries no identity on its own; you attach it to something.

A User is a permanent identity with long-lived credentials, meant for a human or a legacy application that needs its own password or access keys. A Group is not something you log in as; it is a bundle you attach policies to once and then add Users into, so twenty engineers who need the same access all inherit it from one place and a single edit updates them all. A Role is the one people misunderstand most — it is an identity with no permanent credentials that is assumed temporarily through STS, handing back short-lived credentials that expire in about an hour.

The reason Roles matter so much in banking is security. At National Bank of India our statement-generator service runs on EC2 and needs to read the customer-statements bucket. If we embedded an access key in that code and it leaked through a log or a repository, an attacker could use it until a human noticed and rotated it. Instead the EC2 instance assumes a Role, receives temporary credentials automatically, and those credentials rotate on their own, so there is simply no long-lived secret to steal.

The way I explain the effective permissions in an interview is this: a User's permissions are the union of its own inline policies plus every policy on every Group it belongs to, and then any explicit deny overrides everything. If nothing allows the action, the implicit deny applies. So in our setup engineers get read access by being in the Developers group, the service gets the same read access through an assumed Role with no keys in the code, and the policy itself is written once and reused everywhere, which is exactly how you keep a bank's access model both secure and maintainable.
